newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission demands tougher sentences for pimps.
newsitem.headline: Commission demands tougher sentences for pimps.

text.p: Criminals exploiting women for sex should get heavier jail sentences, the European Commission said on Wednesday.

Accusing EU governments of brushing the problem under the carpet, Justice Commissioner Anita Gradin said that while a convicted drugs trafficker could expect 10 years in jail, someone found selling women might get only two.

It was clear that hundreds of thousands of women, mainly from central and eastern Europe but also from Asia and Latin America, were being lured into the European Union with the promise of better lives, the Swedish commissioner said.
Once they got there they were forced into a situation of dependency and made to work as prostitutes.
The low sentences and the fact that proof was more difficult to establish, made trafficking in women attractive.
"Trafficking in women is a growing and very profitable business for those in organised crime," she told a news conference to unveil a Commission Communication and action plan to fight the trade.

The Commission wants EU countries to grant temporary residence permits -- as is currently the case in Belgium and the Netherlands -- to allow women victims of the prostitution trade to testify against their captors.
"A temporary permit of stay is necessary to help the victims to recuperate and to testify against the traffickers," the Commission said in a statement.

It is currently difficult to prosecute pimps and traffickers as the women -- who have often entered the country illegally -- are unwilling to testify for fear of being treated as criminals themselves.
Gradin said that captive women were often mistreated and faced a very real danger of contracting AIDS.

The Commission also intends to provide financial aid for information campaigns in the eastern European countries themselves to spread the word about the dangers of accepting offers of work as waitresses, dancers, hostesses and au pairs in the EU.

It also called for training programmes for immigration and asylum officers, social and health workers and police officers and the setting up of reception and rehabilitation centres in both EU and eastern European countries.
